newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan hints it may halt islands protest flotilla.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan hints it may halt islands protest flotilla.

text.p: Taiwan hinted broadly on Friday it may act to halt a protest voyage to challenge Japan's claim to a disputed East China Sea island group, saying Sunday's private flotilla may be illegal.

The warning, issued after Taiwan-Japan negotiations in Tokyo failed to defuse the emotional sovereignty dispute, suggested Taipei might be planning less-passive responses to increasingly militant and dangerous anti-Japanese protests.
A Hong Kong protest leader died on September 26 in the last attempt by activists to reach the islands claimed by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus and by Japan as the Senkakus.

To date, Taipei has done little but urge civic calm and press Japan to restrain ultra-nationalists who reignited a long-dormant row in July by building a lighthouse and hoisting Japan's flag on the uninhabited islands.
Japanese patrols have repulsed private boats trying to land Hong Kong and Taiwan activists on the islands.
Taipei indicated it now might prevent the next anti-Japanese protest flotilla even from leaving Keelung harbour.

"According to regulations, if port authorities find illegal activities they will definitely mete out punishment," Council of Agriculture official Lee Chien-chuan said via Taiwan's state-run Central News agency.

Lee, whose agency regulates fishing, said fishing boats were not allowed to ferry non-fishermen and that pleasure boats were not allowed beyond 24 nautical miles off Taiwan's shores -- putting the disputed islands far beyond reach.
The islands lie 200 km (125 miles) northeast of Taiwan.
Lee said violators faced fines of up to T$150,000 (US$5,500) and revocation of their commercial fishing licences.
Sunday's sailing and a planned Monday landing attempt were not eligible for marine protection as such service does not extend to pleasure boats violating the 24-mile limit, he said.
Protest leaders assailed Taiwan's hardening stance.
"We're trying to protect the Republic of China!" an activist told state television, referring to the Taiwan government.
"How can they revoke our licences?" he said.
In Tokyo, the Japan government sought to ease tensions with China and Taiwan by saying it would would not recognise the offending lighthouse as part of its maritime safety system.
But Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said the concession did not alter Tokyo's claim of sovereignty to the islands, seized in 1895 as war booty after Japan's defeat of China.
Separately, Taiwan negotiators said they had failed to reach agreement with their Japanese counterparts in talks over fishing rights and other issues stemming from the sovereignty row.
"These are issues that can never be resolved overnight, and no agreement has been reached," Chuang Ming-yao, head of Taiwan's representative office in Tokyo, told reporters.

Tensions have grown as Japanese patrols repelled private boats attempting to land protesters on the islands, triggering popular calls in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and China for a more forceful response from Beijing and Taipei.

Pressure on Japan to defuse tensions escalated with the September 26 death of Hong Kong activist David Chan, who drowned after jumping off a protest ship that had been prevented from putting Chan and colleagues ashore.
